opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly one I've thought about a lot, because it sits right at the intersection of the two communities I care about: classical physical simulation and machine learning.

My view is that we shouldn't think of it as "replace the simulator with a neural network" or "keep the simulator and ignore learning." The most promising direction is a hybrid, where each part does what it's good at.

Physical simulators encode a huge amount of prior knowledge for free. Conservation of momentum, conservation of mass, contact constraints, the structure of elasticity. A neural network has to learn all of that from data, and it usually learns it imperfectly. It might look right on the training distribution, but once you push it a little outside, energy blows up or objects pass through each other. So I think throwing away the physics is wasteful. Those inductive biases are exactly what give you generalization.

On the other hand, real-world systems have a lot of messy effects that are really hard to model from first principles. Friction that isn't quite Coulomb, material properties that vary across a sample, actuator delays, sensor noise, cables, air resistance on a soft object. That's where the sim-to-real gap comes from. And that's where learning is very useful.

So concretely, I see a few layers to this.

The first is making the simulator differentiable. This was a big motivation behind a lot of the work I did on DiffTaichi. If your simulator is differentiable, you can treat physical parameters like stiffness, friction coefficients, damping, as variables and fit them directly to real-world observations with gradient descent. That's system identification, but much more scalable than black-box search. You can calibrate hundreds or thousands of parameters instead of a handful.

The second layer is residual learning. You let the physics simulator produce its prediction, and you train a small neural network to predict the correction, the residual between what the simulator says and what actually happens in reality. The network doesn't have to learn gravity or basic dynamics. It only has to learn the part the model got wrong, which is a much easier problem and needs much less data.

The third is using neural networks inside the simulator as learned constitutive models or learned components. For example, instead of a hand-written stress-strain relationship for some weird material, you can have a network that outputs stress given deformation, but you still plug it into a physically structured solver so the overall system respects conservation laws.

And then, on the control side, differentiable simulation lets you optimize controllers end to end through the physics, which is often far more sample-efficient than pure model-free reinforcement learning. Combined with domain randomization, you get policies that are robust to the remaining uncertainty.

One thing I always emphasize, though, is that the infrastructure matters a lot. None of this works well if the simulator is slow, or if writing a differentiable simulator takes six months of engineering. A big reason I built Taichi was to lower that barrier, so researchers can quickly write high-performance, differentiable simulators and iterate on these hybrid ideas. Research speed is heavily determined by how quickly you can try things.

So to summarize: keep the physics as the backbone, make it differentiable, and use learning to fill in the gaps the physics can't capture. I think that combination is how we'll really close the sim-to-real gap.

r001.rationale: The response says replacing physics with a neural network is wasteful because physical laws provide useful prior knowledge, but it does not argue that reproducing a known law with a neural model is computationally unjustified.

r002.rationale: It proposes residual learning: a neural network predicts the correction between the simulator’s prediction and what happens in reality.

r003.rationale: It proposes a learned constitutive model in which a network maps deformation to stress inside a physically structured solver.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, the sim-to-real gap really comes from two places. One is that our physical models are imperfect — we write down constitutive laws, friction models, contact models, and they're approximations. The other is that even if the model is right, we don't know the parameters: the Young's modulus of this particular piece of foam, the friction coefficient of this particular table surface.

Neural networks can help with both, but I think you have to be careful about how you plug them in. The naive approach is to say, okay, let's just replace the whole simulator with a big neural network and train it on real data. The problem is you throw away everything we know about physics. Momentum conservation, symmetry, all of that has to be relearned from data, and you need enormous amounts of data to get it, and even then it tends to generalize poorly outside the training distribution.

What I find much more promising is making the simulator itself differentiable, and then using neural networks only where our physical knowledge genuinely runs out. That's a lot of what motivated the work on DiffTaichi. If every step of your simulation — the time integration, the collision handling, the material response — is differentiable, then you can treat the simulator as part of the computational graph. You can backpropagate from a mismatch between simulated and real trajectories all the way back to the material parameters, or to a small neural network that's modeling, say, the residual in your contact model that you couldn't write down analytically.

So the structure becomes: hard physics where we trust it, learnable components where we don't, and gradients flowing through the whole thing so you can fit it to real observations. That hybrid tends to be very data-efficient, because the network only has to learn the small correction, not the whole dynamics.

The other thing differentiability gives you is that you can close the loop. You can use real-world data to calibrate the simulator, use the calibrated simulator to train a controller, and then go back to the real system, see where it still diverges, and update again. Each iteration shrinks the gap a bit. Without gradients, every one of those steps is a painful black-box optimization.

I'll also say, from a systems perspective, this is why performance matters so much. If your differentiable simulator is slow, nobody will do system identification with it, because you need thousands of forward and backward passes. So a lot of the engineering effort in Taichi was really about making this practical — getting the compiled kernels fast enough on GPUs that you can afford to run optimization loops over the simulator rather than just demos.

So in short: don't replace physics with neural nets, embed neural nets inside physics, make the whole thing differentiable, and make it fast enough that people actually use it.

r001.rationale: The response warns against replacing the whole simulator with a neural network, but does not argue that using an expensive neural model to reproduce a known, cheaply computed physical law is computationally unjustified.

r002.rationale: It proposes using a small neural network to model residuals in a contact model where the physical description is incomplete, capturing discrepancies between the simulator and real behavior.

r003.rationale: The response mentions constitutive laws and material parameters, but does not propose learning a material’s stress–strain relationship from data for use in the simulator.

astra-6.text:
I think the most promising approach is to combine physics with learning. A physical simulator gives you a useful structure, but there are always things you don’t know precisely: material properties, friction, contact behavior, or how an actuator responds. Neural networks can help us model those parts from real-world data.

For example, if a simulated robot moves differently from the real robot, we can use those observations to identify better parameters or learn a correction to the dynamics. A differentiable simulator can make that process easier because it lets us compute how changes in the model affect the observed motion.

But we should also account for uncertainty. Matching one recorded trajectory doesn’t necessarily mean the simulator will predict a new situation correctly. So I would combine learning with physical constraints, test on different conditions, and train controllers across a range of plausible models. The goal is to make the simulator useful for decisions that transfer to the real world.

r001.rationale: The response does not argue that neural models are unjustified for reproducing cheap, known physical laws.

r002.rationale: It proposes using real-world observations to improve simulator parameters or learn corrections to its dynamics, addressing discrepancies between simulation and reality.

r003.rationale: It mentions material properties generally but does not propose learning a material’s stress–strain relationship from data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful way to approach this is to combine the structure of a physical simulator with the ability of neural networks to learn from data. We already have physical laws that explain a lot of what happens, so we can use those as the foundation. But there are always things we don’t know precisely—material properties, friction, contact behavior—and those can create a gap between simulation and reality.

Neural networks can help model those uncertain parts. If the simulator is differentiable, we can compare its predictions with real observations and use gradients to adjust parameters or train a learned component. That gives us a way to make the simulation more consistent with the measurements.

The important question is whether that improvement carries over to new situations. A model might fit one experiment very well and still fail when the conditions change. So I would focus on learning the parts we cannot model accurately, while keeping the physical structure that helps the simulator generalize.

r001.rationale: The response says to use physical laws as the foundation, but does not argue that reproducing known laws with an expensive neural model is computationally unjustified.

r002.rationale: It proposes using neural networks to model uncertain parts of the simulator, such as material properties, friction, and contact behavior, to better match real observations.

r003.rationale: It mentions material properties but does not propose learning a material’s stress–strain relationship from data for the simulator.
